mode: in place (owner's decision, 2026-10-23: audit and fix in place, not rebuilt on frame-2026-10)
by: Claude (lead dev); independent review of every shipped sentence against its cited source, 2026-10-23 (6 fixes applied: Plato's indirectness and readers' thinking given as two claims; forms 'called forms or ideas' and the Republic's ideal city; Stoic complete works from Imperial-period writers (Epictetus was no Roman author); Cicero's place in the passage to early modern skepticism; Iamblichus's ritual over ascesis; Augustine familiar with the writings)
verdicts: evidence: did one of the article's cited sources support it (yes|partly|no|n/a). accuracy: supported|overstated|contested|wrong|unverified|editorial|non-assertive, settled by the source in 'by'. Excerpts are under 15 words and come from a summarizing fetch, so the reviewer re-reads the section named.

sentences.text: Greek philosophy began early in the sixth century BCE, when Thales, whom Aristotle credits with declaring water the first cause, sought reasoned explanations of nature.

claims.excerpt: the first to engage in such inquiry
claims.note: Curd reports Aristotle's claim that Thales was first; the article states it as when Greek philosophy began.
claims.fix: attribute the claim of priority to Aristotle

sentences.text: Anaximander posited an indefinite originating stuff, the apeiron, and Anaximenes replaced it with air.

claims.excerpt: replaces Anaximander's apeiron with air

sentences.text: Heraclitus wrote of a logos that holds forever, Parmenides argued that what is cannot come to be or perish, and Zeno's paradoxes, extending Parmenides' arguments, purported to show that ordinary motion is impossible.

claims.excerpt: logos which holds forever

sentences.text: Empedocles posited four roots, earth, water, air and fire, Anaxagoras a mixture set in rotation by Mind, and Leucippus and Democritus uncuttable atoms in the void.

claims.excerpt: an infinite number of solid, uncuttable

claims.excerpt: Of all things the measure is man
claims.note: Curd's entry does not give the man-measure fragment; Bonazzi does, and calls Protagoras the most famous sophist.

claims.fix: add citations; call them Imperial-period writers; cut the unsourced clause

sentences.text: Academic skeptics questioned claims to secure knowledge, while Pyrrhonian skeptics, especially as presented by Sextus Empiricus, developed practices of setting opposing arguments against one another and suspending judgment.

claims.excerpt: generates equipollence
claims.note: Sextus is not named in the parts of Vogt's entry retrieved; the method is given for Aenesidemus.

sentences.text: These traditions differed in their aims and arguments.

claims.note: True but empty; Vogt gives the actual difference (tranquility).

sentences.text: Their questions about justification, appearance, and dogmatism continue to inform epistemology.

claims.excerpt: a step toward modern skepticism

sentences.text: Roman authors adapted and disputed Greek philosophical ideas within distinctive literary and political contexts.

claims.note: Generic.

claims.excerpt: the three supra-sensible so-called “hypostases”
claims.note: Kalligas: Plotinus took Plato to have furnished the fundamentals; 'transforming' Platonic arguments is a modern judgment.

sentences.text: Porphyry, Iamblichus, and Proclus developed different metaphysical, religious, and pedagogical projects.

claims.note: Too vague to check; the sources give specific differences.
